headings.title: Introduction and Overview
headings.content: The external female reproductive organs are collectively known as the **vulva** or the **pudendum**. This area serves multiple vital functions, including protecting internal reproductive structures from infection, playing a key role in sexual arousal, and providing the anatomical opening for childbirth and menstruation. Unlike the internal organs such as the uterus and ovaries, the structures of the vulva are entirely visible on the body surface, stretching from the pubic symphysis down to the perineum. Understanding this anatomy is essential for clinical assessment, hygiene education, and identifying pathological changes.

headings.title: Mons Pubis and Labia Majora
headings.content:
- **Mons Pubis**: A rounded, fatty eminence located directly over the pubic bone. After puberty, it becomes covered with pubic hair and contains many sweat and sebaceous glands, serving as a cushion during sexual activity.
- **Labia Majora**: Two prominent, longitudinal folds of skin that extend downward and backward from the mons pubis toward the perineum. They protect the delicate structures lying between them and are homologous to the scrotum in males. The outer surfaces are pigmented and hair-covered, while the inner surfaces are smooth and rich in sebaceous glands.

headings.title: Labia Minora and Interlabial Structures
headings.content: The **labia minora** are two delicate, hairless folds of skin located just inside the labia majora. They lack adipose tissue but contain numerous nerve endings, blood vessels, and sebaceous glands, making them highly sensitive. Anteriorly, the labia minora split to form a fold over and under the clitoris, creating the **prepuce** (clitoral hood) and the frenulum. The space enclosed between the labia minora is called the interlabial space or vestibule.

headings.title: The Clitoris
headings.content: The **clitoris** is a small, cylindrical, highly sensitive erectile organ located at the anterior junction of the labia minora. Its primary physiological function is sexual arousal and pleasure. Anatomically, it consists of a visible **glans**, a body (shaft), and internal crura and bulbs that extend deep into the pelvic tissue. Because it possesses thousands of sensory nerve endings, it is the primary center of female erogenous sensation.

headings.title: The Vestibule and Associated Glands
headings.content: The **vestibule** is the almond-shaped space enclosed by the labia minora. It contains the openings of the urethra, the vagina, and several important glands. The **Bartholin's glands** (greater vestibular glands) are located on either side of the vaginal opening and secrete mucus to lubricate the vulva during sexual arousal. The **Skene's glands** (lesser vestibular glands) sit near the lower end of the urethra and secrete fluid into the urethral opening.

headings.title: The Vaginal Orifice and Hymen
headings.content: The **vaginal orifice** (introitus) is the external opening into the vagina, varying in size and appearance depending on age and previous stretching. Surrounding or partially covering this opening is the **hymen**, a thin fold of mucous membrane. The hymen can take many shapes, such as annular, cribriform, or septate. A common clinical misconception is that an intact hymen proves virginity; however, the hymen can be stretched or torn due to strenuous physical exercise, tampon use, or injury, making it an unreliable indicator of sexual history.

headings.title: Blood Supply, Innervation, and Lymphatic Drainage
headings.content: The vulva has an exceptionally rich vascular supply, primarily derived from the internal and external pudendal arteries, which explains why lacerations in this area bleed profusely. Sensory innervation is supplied by the pudendal nerve as well as branches of the ilioinguinal and posterior cutaneous nerves of the thigh. This high concentration of nerves makes perineal trauma extremely painful. **Lymphatic drainage** from the external genitalia flows primarily to the superficial inguinal lymph nodes, an important clinical pathway when assessing for infections or malignancies of the vulva.

headings.title: Clinical Significance and Nursing Assessment
headings.content: Nursing assessment of the external female reproductive organs requires cultural sensitivity, clear communication, and proper positioning, typically the lithotomy position. The nurse inspects the vulva for symmetry, color, skin integrity, swelling, lesions, discharge, and signs of trauma or infection. Because patients may feel vulnerable or anxious during this examination, explaining each step before touching the patient is essential to build trust and reduce anxiety.
